questions.q: How does List<T> work internally, and what are the real costs of Add, Insert and Remove?
questions.a:
{{List<T>}} wraps a contiguous array {{_items}} plus a {{_size}} count.

- **Add**: amortised O(1). When full, it allocates a new array of double capacity and copies (O(n) for that call). Doubling makes the average cost per add constant.
- **Insert/RemoveAt in the middle**: O(n), because elements shift ({{Array.Copy}}).
- **Index access**: O(1), bounds-checked.
- **Contains / IndexOf**: O(n) linear scan using {{EqualityComparer<T>.Default}}.
- **Remove(item)**: O(n) search + shift.

Hidden costs: growth copies and the old arrays become garbage; arrays over 85,000 bytes land on the Large Object Heap. Pre-size with the constructor capacity when the count is known, and use {{CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)}} for allocation-free iteration in hot paths (do not modify the list while holding the span).
questions.code:
~~~csharp
var trades = new List<Trade>(capacity: expectedCount);   // avoids log2(n) regrow-and-copy steps
foreach (var t in source) trades.Add(t);                  // amortised O(1)

trades.Insert(0, first);                                  // O(n): shifts every element
trades.RemoveAt(0);                                       // O(n)
var q = new Queue<Trade>();                               // use a queue for FIFO instead: O(1) both ends

Span<Trade> span = CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(trades);    // no enumerator allocation, no version checks
decimal notional = 0; foreach (ref readonly var t in span) notional += t.Price * t.Qty;
~~~
pts: List<T> is a growable array; Add is amortised O(1) through capacity doubling.
Insert and remove in the middle are O(n) because elements shift.
Contains and IndexOf are linear scans.
Pre-size when the count is known to avoid copies and LOH churn.
CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan gives allocation-free iteration on hot paths.
questions.ex: A pricing job removing items from the front of a 2-million-element List took 40 minutes (O(n²)); switching to a Queue made it seconds.

What happens if you modify a list during foreach?

Calling Contains inside a loop over another list (O(n·m)).

questions.q: How does Dictionary<TKey,TValue> work, and what makes lookups O(1) or not?
questions.a:
.NET's {{Dictionary}} uses **separate chaining with arrays**: a {{buckets}} array of indices into an {{entries}} array; each entry stores hash code, key, value and {{next}} index for collisions.

Lookup: compute {{GetHashCode()}}, map to a bucket (modulo a prime size, or fast modulo), walk the chain comparing hash codes then {{Equals}}.

O(1) average requires:

- A **good hash distribution**: a constant or poorly distributed {{GetHashCode}} degrades to O(n) chains.
- **Immutable keys** while stored: mutating a key's hashed fields loses the entry.
- A reasonable load: it resizes (to the next prime above double) when full; resizing rehashes everything (O(n)).

Since .NET Core, string keys use **randomised hashing** per process, which defends against hash-flooding DoS. Pass the right comparer ({{StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase}}) rather than lower-casing keys.

### Load factor, resizing and hash flooding
- **Load factor** = entries / buckets. As it rises, chains get longer and lookups slow down. .NET's Dictionary resizes to the next prime roughly double the size when its entry array is full, rehashing every key: an O(n) step that is amortised O(1) per insert, but a visible pause and big allocation for millions of entries. Pass a capacity when you know the size.
- **Bad hash codes** destroy O(1): a {{GetHashCode}} that returns the same value for many keys turns the table into a list. Use {{HashCode.Combine}} over the fields that define equality, and never hash mutable fields.
- **Hash flooding**: an attacker who can choose keys (query string names, JSON property names) can force collisions and make each request O(n squared). .NET randomises string hashing per process, which is why string hash codes differ between runs; never persist them.

~~~csharp
public readonly record struct AccountKey(string SortCode, string Number);   // records generate Equals and GetHashCode

var balances = new Dictionary<AccountKey, decimal>(capacity: 2_000_000);  // no rehashing while loading

// Manual implementation when you need one
public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(SortCode, Number);
~~~

questions.q: Explain Big-O for common operations across arrays, linked lists, hash tables, balanced trees and heaps. Why does Big-O not tell the whole story?
questions.a:
| Structure | Access by index | Search | Insert | Delete | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Array / List<T> | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) end*, O(n) middle | O(n) | Cache-friendly |
| Linked list | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) at known node | O(1) at known node | Pointer chasing |
| Hash table | n/a | O(1) avg, O(n) worst | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | No ordering |
| Balanced BST (SortedDictionary) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Ordered, range queries |
| Binary heap (PriorityQueue) | n/a | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) min | Peek min O(1) |
| Sorted array | O(1) | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) | Fast read, slow write |

(* amortised)

Big-O hides **constants and memory behaviour**: an array scan of 1,000 items can beat a hash lookup with an expensive hash; linked lists lose to arrays in practice because of cache misses; allocations and GC matter in .NET. Measure with BenchmarkDotNet for real decisions, and consider data size, access pattern and concurrency.
pts: Know the table: arrays O(1) index, hash O(1) average, trees O(log n), heaps O(log n) insert.
Hash tables give no ordering; trees give ordering and range queries.
Big-O hides constants, cache locality and allocation costs.
Small n often favours simple arrays.
Benchmark real decisions.

questions.q: Stacks and queues: implementations in .NET and real uses. Solve "valid parentheses".
questions.a:
- **Stack<T>** (LIFO): array-backed, push/pop O(1) amortised. Uses: undo history, expression parsing, DFS, call-stack simulation, matching brackets.
- **Queue<T>** (FIFO): circular buffer, enqueue/dequeue O(1) amortised. Uses: BFS, work queues, rate-limiting windows.
- **PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>** (.NET 6+): binary min-heap. Uses: schedulers, Dijkstra, top-K.
- **Concurrent** variants: {{ConcurrentQueue<T>}}, {{ConcurrentStack<T>}}, and {{Channel<T>}} for async producer/consumer with backpressure.

Valid parentheses: push opening brackets, pop on closing and check the match; the string is valid if the stack is empty at the end. O(n) time, O(n) space.
pts: Stack is LIFO, Queue is FIFO; both O(1) amortised and array-backed.
PriorityQueue is a binary heap for schedulers and Dijkstra.
Use ConcurrentQueue or Channel for concurrent producers and consumers.
Bracket matching: push opens, pop on close, empty at the end.
O(n) time and O(n) space.

questions.q: Solve Two Sum in O(n), then explain how HashSet/Dictionary make many "find a pair" problems linear.
questions.a:
Brute force checks every pair: O(n²). The linear approach stores each number's index in a dictionary; for each element, check whether {{target - x}} was already seen.

Pattern: **trade space for time with a hash structure** ("complement lookup"). It generalises to:

- Detect duplicates ({{HashSet.Add}} returns false).
- Subarray sum equals k (prefix sums in a dictionary).
- First non-repeating character (count map).
- Anagram grouping (sorted key or frequency signature as the dictionary key).

If the input is sorted, a **two-pointer** approach gives O(n) time and O(1) space instead.
pts: Store seen values in a dictionary and look up the complement: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Brute force is O(n²).
The pattern generalises to duplicates, prefix sums and anagrams.
For sorted input, two pointers give O(1) space.
Clarify duplicates and whether indices or values are required.

Return all pairs, not just one?

questions.q: Why are strings immutable in .NET, and how do you build and parse strings efficiently?
questions.a:
Strings are immutable UTF-16 sequences: every modification creates a new string. Benefits: thread safety, safe dictionary keys, interning, security (a validated string cannot change).

Costs: concatenation in a loop is O(n²) in copying and allocations.

Efficient options:

- {{StringBuilder}}: mutable buffer for repeated appends.
- {{string.Create}} / {{string.Join}} / interpolated string handlers (C# 10 builds interpolations efficiently).
- **Spans** ({{ReadOnlySpan<char>}}) for parsing and slicing without allocating substrings: {{MemoryExtensions.Split}} (.NET 9), {{int.Parse(span)}}.
- {{SearchValues<char>}} (.NET 8) for fast multi-character searches.
- Ordinal comparisons ({{StringComparison.Ordinal}}) for identifiers: faster and culture-independent.
pts: Strings are immutable: safe to share and use as keys.
Concatenation in a loop is O(n²); use StringBuilder.
Spans parse and slice without allocating substrings.
SearchValues and ordinal comparisons speed up searching.
Use invariant culture for machine-readable formats.

questions.q: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Implement it in C#.
questions.a:
Combine a **hash map** (key -> node) for O(1) lookup with a **doubly linked list** ordered by recency for O(1) move-to-front and evict-from-back.

- Get: find node in the map, move it to the front, return value.
- Put: if present, update and move to front; else add to front, and if over capacity remove the tail node and its map entry.

Production considerations: thread safety (lock, or sharded caches), memory bounds by size not count, TTLs, and stampede protection. In real .NET services you would use {{MemoryCache}} (size limits, expiration) or {{HybridCache}}; the LRU implementation tests data-structure fluency.

questions.q: Find the top K most frequent items in a large stream. Compare heap, sorting and bucket approaches.
questions.a:
Step 1: count frequencies with a dictionary (O(n)).

Step 2 options:

- **Sort all distinct items** by count: O(m log m) for m distinct items. Simple.
- **Min-heap of size K**: push each item; if the heap exceeds K, pop the minimum. O(m log K): much better when K is small.
- **Bucket sort** by frequency (index = count): O(m) when counts are bounded by n.
- **Streaming / bounded memory**: Count-Min Sketch + heap, or Space-Saving algorithm for approximate heavy hitters (Redis Top-K, analytics systems).

.NET's {{PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>}} is a min-heap.
pts: Count frequencies first with a dictionary.
A size-K min-heap gives O(m log K).
Sorting is O(m log m); bucket sort can be O(m).
For unbounded streams use approximate structures (Count-Min, Space-Saving).
PriorityQueue in .NET is a min-heap.

questions.q: Binary search trees vs balanced trees (red-black, AVL, B-trees): what does SortedDictionary use, and when do you need ordering?
questions.a:
A plain **BST** gives O(log n) only when balanced; sorted inserts degrade it to a linked list (O(n)). **Self-balancing** trees fix this:

- **Red-black trees**: looser balance, fewer rotations on insert/delete. .NET's {{SortedDictionary}} and {{SortedSet}} are red-black trees.
- **AVL trees**: stricter balance, faster lookups, more rotations.
- **B-trees / B+trees**: high fan-out nodes sized to disk pages; minimise I/O. Used by databases (SQL Server, PostgreSQL indexes) and file systems.

{{SortedList<K,V>}} is a sorted array: O(log n) lookup, O(n) insert, compact memory, fast for read-mostly data.

Use ordered structures when you need: range queries (all prices between x and y), min/max, ordered iteration, floor/ceiling (nearest key). Otherwise a hash table is faster.

questions.q: Represent a graph and implement BFS and DFS. When do you use each in real systems?
questions.a:
Representations:

- **Adjacency list** ({{Dictionary<Node, List<Node>>}}): O(V + E) memory; standard for sparse graphs.
- **Adjacency matrix**: O(V²) memory; O(1) edge check; dense graphs only.

Traversals, both O(V + E):

- **BFS** (queue): shortest path in unweighted graphs, level-by-level exploration ("degrees of separation", nearest available driver in hops).
- **DFS** (stack/recursion): reachability, cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.

Real uses: dependency resolution (build/deploy order via topological sort), fraud rings (connected components of shared devices/cards), org hierarchies, network routing, permission inheritance.

Watch recursion depth in DFS on large graphs (use an explicit stack) and always track visited nodes.
pts: Adjacency lists for sparse graphs, matrices for dense ones.
BFS with a queue finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS with a stack finds reachability, cycles, components and topological order.
Both are O(V + E) with a visited set.
Use an explicit stack to avoid recursion depth limits.

questions.q: Implement a trie for prefix search / autocomplete. What are its memory trade-offs?
questions.a:
A **trie** stores strings character by character; each node has children keyed by character and a flag for "end of word". Insert and lookup cost O(L) where L is the word length, independent of how many words are stored. Prefix search walks to the prefix node then enumerates its subtree.

Trade-offs:

- Memory heavy: a node per character with a child map. Compress with **radix trees** (merge single-child chains) or use arrays for small alphabets.
- Great for autocomplete, IP routing (longest prefix match), dictionary checks, BIN-range lookups.
- For large-scale search, an inverted index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) or a sorted array with binary search for prefixes is often simpler.

For top-N suggestions, store the top-N popular completions at each node to avoid subtree traversal.
pts: A trie stores strings by character path; lookup is O(L) in word length.
Prefix search walks to the prefix node then enumerates.
Memory heavy; radix trees compress single-child chains.
Used for autocomplete, longest-prefix match, BIN-range lookups.
At scale, inverted indexes or sorted arrays may be simpler.

questions.q: Solve "longest substring without repeating characters" and explain the sliding-window pattern.
questions.a:
A **sliding window** maintains a range [left, right] over a sequence and moves the boundaries to keep an invariant, avoiding re-scanning: each element enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n).

For the longest substring without repeats: extend {{right}}; if the character was seen inside the window, move {{left}} to one past its last position; track the max window length. A dictionary (or an int array for ASCII) stores last positions.

The pattern solves: max sum subarray of size k, smallest subarray with sum >= target, rate limiting over time windows, moving averages, and "at most K distinct" problems.
pts: A sliding window moves left and right bounds to keep an invariant.
Each element enters and leaves once: O(n).
Track last positions to jump the left bound past duplicates.
Fixed windows subtract the element leaving and add the one entering.
The pattern applies to rate limits, moving averages and constrained subarrays.
questions.ex: A velocity check ("more than 5 transactions in 10 minutes") used a sliding window over each card's ordered timestamps.

pit: Moving left backwards when the duplicate is outside the window.

questions.q: Immutable and frozen collections in .NET: ImmutableList, ImmutableArray, FrozenDictionary. When do you use each?
questions.a:
- **ImmutableArray<T>**: a struct wrapping an array; O(1) index, very fast reads, but every "modification" copies the whole array (O(n)). Best for small or rarely changed data shared across threads.
- **ImmutableList<T> / ImmutableDictionary**: persistent balanced trees; "modifications" return a new version sharing most nodes (O(log n)), but reads are slower (pointer chasing) than arrays/hash tables. Best when you need many versions or frequent copy-on-write updates.
- **FrozenDictionary / FrozenSet** (.NET 8): built once, optimised for read speed (analyses keys to pick an optimal hashing strategy). Expensive to create, fastest lookups. Best for configuration and reference data loaded at startup.
- **ReadOnlyCollection / IReadOnlyList**: read-only **views** over mutable collections, not immutable.

Thread-safe publication: swap a reference to a new immutable/frozen instance atomically ({{Volatile.Write}} or {{Interlocked.Exchange}}) when reference data refreshes.
pts: ImmutableArray: fastest immutable reads, O(n) per change.
ImmutableList/Dictionary: persistent trees, cheap versions, slower reads.
FrozenDictionary/FrozenSet: slow to build, fastest lookups for static data.
ReadOnlyCollection is a view, not immutable.
Refresh reference data by atomically swapping a new instance.
questions.ex: Switching a BIN lookup table from Dictionary to FrozenDictionary cut lookup time by about 40% on a path called 20,000 times per second.
fu: What is structural sharing?
pit: Using ImmutableList in hot read paths expecting array speed.

questions.q: ConcurrentDictionary internals and pitfalls: when is it the right tool?
questions.a:
{{ConcurrentDictionary}} uses **fine-grained lock striping** for writes (a lock per group of buckets) and **lock-free reads**. Reads never block; writes to different stripes proceed in parallel.

Pitfalls:

- **GetOrAdd / AddOrUpdate factories may run more than once** under contention (only one result is stored). Wrap expensive or side-effecting factories in {{Lazy<T>}}.
- **Compound operations are not atomic**: check-then-act across two calls races. Use the atomic APIs ({{TryAdd}}, {{TryUpdate}} with comparison, {{AddOrUpdate}}).
- **Count, Keys, Values, ToArray** take all locks: expensive and blocking; avoid in hot paths.
- **Enumeration** is safe but not a snapshot (may see concurrent changes).
- Values that are mutable objects still need their own synchronisation.

Alternatives: immutable snapshots with atomic swap for read-mostly data; {{Channel<T>}} for producer/consumer; sharding by key into single-threaded owners (actors).
pts: Lock-striped writes and lock-free reads.
GetOrAdd factories can run more than once: wrap in Lazy.
Use the atomic APIs; check-then-act races.
Count, Keys and ToArray take all locks.
Mutable values still need their own synchronisation.

questions.q: Merge overlapping intervals and detect booking conflicts. What structure do you use at scale?
questions.a:
### Merge intervals
Sort by start (O(n log n)), then sweep: if the next interval starts before the current one ends, extend the end; otherwise emit the current and start a new one.

### Conflict check for one new booking
With intervals sorted by start, binary search for the neighbours and check overlap (O(log n)). In a sorted tree ({{SortedSet}} with a comparer), find floor and ceiling.

### At scale
- **Interval trees** answer "which intervals overlap X" in O(log n + k).
- **Databases**: PostgreSQL range types with GiST exclusion constraints guarantee no overlaps under concurrency; SQL Server needs a check with locking or a unique slot model.
- **Discretised slots** (15-minute buckets) turn overlap checks into unique-key inserts, simple and concurrency-safe.

Remember half-open intervals [start, end) so back-to-back bookings do not conflict.
pts: Sort by start, then sweep and extend overlapping ends.
Use half-open intervals so adjacent bookings do not clash.
Interval trees answer overlap queries in O(log n + k).
Let the database enforce no-overlap (exclusion constraints) under concurrency.
Discrete slots turn overlap checks into unique inserts.

questions.q: Arrays of structs vs arrays of classes: how does memory layout affect performance?
questions.a:
- **Array of classes**: the array holds references; each object lives elsewhere on the heap with a header (~16 bytes on 64-bit) plus fields. Iterating chases pointers, causing cache misses; each object is GC-tracked.
- **Array of structs**: values stored contiguously inline. Iteration is sequential memory access (CPU prefetching), no per-element headers, and no GC tracking for the elements (if the struct contains no references).

Use structs for small, immutable, value-like data in large collections (ticks, points, money amounts). Keep them small (16 bytes is a common guideline), make them {{readonly}}, and pass large ones by {{in}}/{{ref}} to avoid copies.

**Structure of arrays** (separate arrays per field) can beat array of structs when you only read a few fields (column-oriented, like columnstore indexes), and enables SIMD.
pts: Arrays of classes hold references to scattered objects; scans miss the cache.
Arrays of structs are contiguous, header-free and GC-light.
Keep structs small, readonly and pass large ones by in or ref.
Structure of arrays wins when reading few fields and enables SIMD.
Measure with BenchmarkDotNet before redesigning.

questions.q: Prefix sums: solve "count subarrays summing to K" and explain where prefix sums appear in production.
questions.a:
A **prefix sum** array {{P[i] = a[0] + ... + a[i-1]}} turns any range sum into {{P[r] - P[l]}} in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

Subarrays summing to K: a subarray (l, r] sums to K when {{P[r] - P[l] = K}}. Walk once, keep a dictionary counting how many times each prefix value occurred, and for each new prefix add the count of {{prefix - K}}. O(n) time and space, and works with negative numbers (unlike sliding windows).

Production equivalents: running balances (prefix sums of transactions), cumulative metrics, summed-area tables for 2D ranges, Fenwick/segment trees when values update.

Count subarrays summing to K with a dictionary of prefix counts.
Works with negative numbers, unlike sliding windows.

questions.q: When do you need a Fenwick tree or segment tree instead of prefix sums?
questions.a:
Prefix sums are static: an update at position i forces rebuilding O(n) prefix values. When values change and you still need fast range queries:

- **Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree)**: point update and prefix query in O(log n), tiny code, O(n) memory. Supports sums (and other invertible operations).
- **Segment tree**: range query and point update in O(log n) for any associative operation (sum, min, max, gcd); with **lazy propagation**, also range updates in O(log n).

Use cases: live leaderboards by score buckets, order-book depth by price level with frequent updates, rolling analytics, rate counters over buckets.

In production, often a database, Redis sorted sets, or columnstore handles this; implement these trees for in-memory hot paths (matching engines, risk aggregation) or interviews.

Fenwick trees: point update and prefix query in O(log n).

Use them for frequently updated range aggregates in memory.

questions.q: Why do databases use B+trees, and how does that explain index design rules?
questions.a:
A **B+tree** keeps keys sorted in nodes sized to a disk page (8 KB in SQL Server/PostgreSQL). High fan-out (hundreds of keys per node) means a billion rows need only 3 to 4 levels, so a lookup is 3 to 4 page reads, most of them cached. Leaf pages are linked, making range scans sequential.

This explains classic index rules:

- **Seek vs scan**: a seek walks root to leaf (O(log n)); a scan reads leaves.
- **Composite key order**: the tree is sorted by the first column, then the second; equality columns first, range columns last.
- **Narrow keys**: more keys per page, fewer levels, smaller indexes (and the clustering key is copied into every non-clustered index in SQL Server).
- **Random keys (GUIDv4)** insert into random leaf pages: page splits, fragmentation, cache misses; sequential keys append at the right edge.
- **Covering indexes** avoid the extra lookup from leaf to base row.

questions.q: What is an LSM-tree and why do Cassandra, RocksDB and Kafka-like systems favour append-only structures?
questions.a:
A **Log-Structured Merge tree** buffers writes in an in-memory sorted structure (memtable) and a write-ahead log; when full, the memtable is flushed as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Background **compaction** merges SSTables, discarding overwritten and deleted keys (tombstones).

Why append-only:

- **Writes are sequential**: much faster than random B-tree page updates, especially on disks and with high write rates.
- **Immutability** simplifies concurrency, replication and snapshots.

Costs:

- **Read amplification**: a key may be in several SSTables; mitigated by **Bloom filters** per SSTable and caches.
- **Write amplification** from compaction; **space amplification** before compaction.
- Compaction storms can hurt latency.

B-trees (SQL Server, PostgreSQL) favour read-heavy, update-in-place OLTP; LSM-trees (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB, DynamoDB's storage, many time-series stores) favour write-heavy workloads. Kafka is a simpler append-only log with segment files and offset indexes.

Write path:  client -> WAL (sequential append) -> memtable (sorted, in memory)
             memtable full -> flush to SSTable L0 (immutable, sorted)
             compaction: L0+L1 -> merged L1 (drops overwritten keys and expired tombstones)
Read path:   memtable -> (Bloom filter says "maybe") SSTable L0 -> L1 -> ... first hit wins
~~~

questions.q: How does a Bloom filter work, how do you size it, and where would you use one?
questions.a:
A **Bloom filter** is a bit array of m bits with k hash functions. Insert sets k bits; a query checks those k bits: if any is 0 the item is **definitely absent**; if all are 1 it is **probably present** (false positives possible, false negatives impossible). No deletes (use a counting or Cuckoo filter for that).

Sizing for n items and false-positive rate p:

- m = -n ln p / (ln 2)² bits; k = (m / n) ln 2.
- About **9.6 bits per item for 1%**, 14.4 bits for 0.1%.

Uses:

- Skip disk reads for absent keys (LSM-tree SSTables, Cassandra, RocksDB).
- Cache penetration protection (reject lookups for ids that do not exist).
- Deduplication of crawled URLs or processed event ids (with acceptable false positives).
- "Has this password appeared in breaches?" checks client-side.

questions.q: Explain consistent hashing with virtual nodes. Why not just use hash(key) mod N?
questions.a:
With {{hash(key) mod N}}, changing N (adding or removing a server) remaps almost **every** key: caches go cold, data must move massively.

**Consistent hashing** maps both servers and keys onto a ring (hash space). A key belongs to the first server clockwise. Adding or removing a server only moves the keys in the affected arc: about 1/N of keys.

**Virtual nodes**: each physical server gets many points on the ring (e.g. 100 to 200). This smooths load distribution, and when a server leaves, its keys spread across many servers rather than one neighbour. Weighting (more vnodes) handles heterogeneous capacity.

Used by Cassandra, DynamoDB (internally), Redis Cluster (with fixed hash slots, a related idea), CDNs, sharded caches, and load balancers with session affinity. **Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing** is a simpler alternative with similar properties.

questions.q: What is a skip list, and why does Redis use one for sorted sets?
questions.a:
A **skip list** is a sorted linked list with extra "express lane" levels: each node is promoted to higher levels with probability p (typically 1/2 or 1/4). Search starts at the top level and drops down, giving **expected O(log n)** search, insert and delete.

Why Redis uses it for sorted sets (combined with a hash table for member -> score):

- Simple to implement and reason about compared with balanced trees.
- Efficient **range operations** (ZRANGEBYSCORE) by walking the bottom level.
- Rank queries supported by storing span widths per link.
- Good concurrency properties in lock-free variants (Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap).

Trade-offs: probabilistic balance (worst case O(n) is astronomically unlikely), more pointers per node than a tree.

questions.q: Ring buffers: how do they work and why are they used in high-performance systems (logging, market data, the LMAX Disruptor)?
questions.a:
A **ring buffer** is a fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap around (index mod capacity, or bit-masking when capacity is a power of two). Writes and reads are O(1) with no allocations after construction.

Why high-performance systems use them:

- **No GC pressure**: slots are preallocated and reused.
- **Cache-friendly** sequential memory.
- **Bounded**: natural backpressure or overwrite-oldest semantics.
- **Single-producer/single-consumer** variants can be lock-free with memory barriers only.

Examples: the LMAX Disruptor (trading), audio buffers, in-memory "last N" logs, network card queues, {{Queue<T>}} itself (a growable circular buffer), and {{System.Threading.Channels}} bounded channels conceptually.

Pitfalls: overwrite policy must be explicit; false sharing between head and tail counters (pad them onto separate cache lines).

pts: Fixed array with wrapping head and tail: O(1), zero allocations.
Power-of-two capacity allows bit-mask indexing.
Bounded by design: backpressure or overwrite-oldest.
SPSC variants are lock-free with memory barriers.
Watch false sharing between counters.

questions.q: Topological sort: solve dependency ordering (builds, migrations, service startup) and detect cycles.
questions.a:
A **topological order** of a directed acyclic graph lists nodes so every edge goes from earlier to later. **Kahn's algorithm**:

1. Compute in-degrees.
2. Queue all nodes with in-degree 0.
3. Pop a node, append to the order, decrement neighbours' in-degrees, enqueue those reaching 0.
4. If the order contains fewer nodes than the graph, there is a **cycle**.

O(V + E). Using a priority queue instead of a queue gives a deterministic order (useful for reproducible builds).

Production uses: build systems (MSBuild project graph), database migration ordering, Terraform resource graphs, Helm/Kubernetes dependency startup, task schedulers (DAGs in Airflow), spreadsheet recalculation.
pts: Topological order puts every dependency before its dependants.
Kahn's algorithm uses in-degrees and a queue: O(V + E).
Leftover nodes mean a cycle; report them.
A priority queue makes the order deterministic.
Used by build systems, migrations, Terraform and DAG schedulers.
questions.ex: A deployment orchestrator for 60 microservices computed startup waves with Kahn's algorithm and failed fast with the cycle members listed when a team introduced a circular dependency.
fu: How do you compute parallel "waves" of independent tasks?
pit: Silently returning a partial order when a cycle exists.

questions.q: Implement Dijkstra's shortest path. Where does it apply in business systems, and when do you need A* or Bellman-Ford?
questions.a:
**Dijkstra** finds shortest paths from a source in graphs with **non-negative** weights: repeatedly take the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance (min-heap) and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

- **A***: Dijkstra plus a heuristic estimating remaining distance (straight-line distance on maps); explores far fewer nodes for point-to-point routing.
- **Bellman-Ford**: handles **negative weights** and detects negative cycles: O(VE). Classic finance use: **currency arbitrage** detection (weights = -log(rate); a negative cycle means arbitrage).

Business uses: delivery routing, network latency routing, cheapest payment routing across rails/correspondent banks (cost as weight), supply-chain lead times.
pts: Dijkstra: min-heap of tentative distances, non-negative weights only.
O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.
A* adds a heuristic for faster point-to-point routing.
Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.
Negative cycles in -log(rate) graphs reveal FX arbitrage.
questions.ex: A cross-border payments router chose the cheapest correspondent-bank path with Dijkstra on fee-plus-spread weights, saving basis points on every transfer.
fu: How would you include time-of-day cut-off windows?
pit: Using Dijkstra with negative edge weights.

questions.q: What is Union-Find (disjoint set), and where does it beat graph traversal?
questions.a:
**Union-Find** maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets with two operations:

- {{Find(x)}}: representative of x's set.
- {{Union(a, b)}}: merge the sets.

With **path compression** and **union by rank/size**, both run in nearly constant amortised time (inverse Ackermann).

It beats repeated BFS/DFS when edges arrive **incrementally** and you need connectivity answers along the way: entity resolution (merge customer records sharing email/phone/device), fraud ring detection as links stream in, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, network connectivity, grouping duplicate accounts.

It does not support splitting sets efficiently; for deletions you rebuild or use other structures.
pts: Union-Find tracks disjoint sets with Find and Union.
Path compression plus union by size gives near-constant amortised time.
Ideal for incremental connectivity as links arrive.
Used in entity resolution, fraud clustering and Kruskal's MST.
It does not support splitting sets.
questions.ex: A KYC team merged 30 million customer records into identity clusters by unioning on shared emails, phones and devices in minutes.
fu: How would you distribute this over a cluster?
pit: No path compression, giving long chains.

questions.q: Compare LRU, LFU, FIFO, TTL and W-TinyLFU eviction. Which do you choose for which workload?
questions.a:
- **FIFO**: evict oldest inserted; cheap, ignores access patterns.
- **LRU**: evict least recently used; good for recency-heavy workloads; vulnerable to **scan pollution** (one big scan evicts the hot set).
- **LFU**: evict least frequently used; protects popular items; slow to adapt when popularity shifts unless counts decay.
- **TTL**: time-based expiry; required for correctness of stale data regardless of policy.
- **W-TinyLFU** (Caffeine in Java; similar ideas in modern caches): a small LRU "window" for new items plus a frequency sketch (Count-Min) admission filter for the main segment; near-optimal hit rates across workloads and scan resistant.
- **ARC / 2Q**: balance recency and frequency with ghost lists.

.NET {{MemoryCache}} evicts by priority, expiration and compaction percentage (not pure LRU); Redis offers approximated LRU and LFU ({{allkeys-lfu}}). Choose LFU-like policies for skewed popularity (product catalogue), LRU for session-like recency, and always TTLs for freshness.

questions.q: How would you store and query relationships for fraud detection (shared devices, cards, addresses)? Graph database or relational?
questions.a:
Model: entities (accounts, cards, devices, addresses, IPs) as nodes and "used"/"shares" as edges. Questions: "accounts within 2 hops of a known fraudster", "connected components above size 10", "new account linked to a device seen with chargebacks".

Options:

- **Relational with recursive CTEs or adjacency tables**: fine for 1 to 2 hops with good indexes; deeper traversals get expensive.
- **Graph database** (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, Azure Cosmos DB Gremlin, TigerGraph): index-free adjacency makes multi-hop traversals fast; good for interactive investigation and real-time 2 to 3 hop checks.
- **In-memory structures** (adjacency lists, Union-Find for components) computed in batch/stream jobs for features fed into ML models.

Typical architecture: events stream into a graph store and a feature store; real-time scoring uses precomputed features (component size, distance to known fraud) plus limited hops; investigators use the graph DB UI.

-- Relational: accounts within 2 hops of a flagged account via shared devices
WITH hop1 AS (SELECT DISTINCT u2.AccountId FROM DeviceUse u1 JOIN DeviceUse u2 ON u2.DeviceId = u1.DeviceId WHERE u1.AccountId = @flagged),
     hop2 AS (SELECT DISTINCT u4.AccountId FROM hop1 h JOIN DeviceUse u3 ON u3.AccountId = h.AccountId JOIN DeviceUse u4 ON u4.DeviceId = u3.DeviceId)
SELECT AccountId FROM hop1 UNION SELECT AccountId FROM hop2;
~~~
~~~text
// Cypher (Neo4j): same question, any depth up to 3
MATCH (f:Account {id: $flagged})-[:USED*1..3]-(a:Account) WHERE a <> f RETURN DISTINCT a.id
~~~
pts: Model entities as nodes and shared usage as edges.
Relational works for shallow hops with good indexes.
Graph databases make multi-hop traversals fast.
Precompute graph features (component size, distance to fraud) for real-time scoring.
Investigators need an interactive graph view.

fu: How do you keep graph features fresh in real time?
pit: Running deep traversals synchronously in the payment authorisation path.

questions.q: Which data structures suit time-series data (metrics, ticks), and how do TSDBs compress it?
questions.a:
Characteristics: append-mostly, ordered by time, queried by ranges and aggregates, huge volume.

Structures and techniques:

- **Time-partitioned chunks** (hourly/daily blocks) for retention by dropping chunks.
- **Columnar layout** per series: timestamps and values stored separately.
- **Delta-of-delta encoding** for timestamps (regular intervals compress to almost nothing).
- **XOR (Gorilla) compression** for floating values: consecutive values often share bits; Facebook's Gorilla achieves ~1.37 bytes per point.
- **Downsampling / rollups** (1s -> 1m -> 1h) with retention per resolution.
- **Inverted index on labels/tags** to find series (Prometheus).
- **Ring buffers** for in-memory recent windows.

Products: Prometheus/Mimir, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL hypertables), Azure Data Explorer, kdb+ in trading, MongoDB time-series collections.

Values: 101.25, 101.25, 101.26 -> XOR with previous: 0, small bit pattern -> few bits per value

ALTER TABLE ticks SET (timescaledb.compress, timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'symbol');
SELECT add_compression_policy('ticks', interval '7 days');

Partition into time chunks for retention.

Downsample to rollups with tiered retention.

pit: Unbounded label cardinality (user ids as labels).

questions.q: What is a Merkle tree, and where is it used (replication, audit logs, blockchains)?
questions.a:
A **Merkle tree** hashes data blocks at the leaves; each parent hashes its children; the root hash summarises the whole dataset. Properties:

- Any change in a leaf changes the root: **tamper evidence**.
- Two replicas can find differences by comparing roots, then only descending into subtrees whose hashes differ: **O(log n) comparisons** to locate divergent ranges (anti-entropy repair in Cassandra and DynamoDB-style systems).
- **Inclusion proofs**: prove an item is in the set with log n sibling hashes (Certificate Transparency logs, blockchains, git objects).

Financial uses: tamper-evident audit logs (publish daily root hashes), proving that an exported ledger matches the system of record, efficient reconciliation between large datasets.

  H34 --> H3[H3 = hash tx3]

Any change alters the root: tamper evidence.
Replicas find divergent ranges in O(log n) comparisons.

questions.q: How do you index spatial data for "nearby" queries (geohash, quadtree, R-tree, H3)?
questions.a:
- **Geohash**: interleaves latitude/longitude bits into a base-32 string; shared prefixes mean nearby cells. Easy to index with B-trees and prefixes. Edge cases at cell boundaries: query the cell plus its 8 neighbours.
- **Quadtree**: recursively splits space into four quadrants; adapts to density (more splits where points cluster).
- **R-tree**: groups nearby objects into bounding rectangles; great for shapes and polygons (PostGIS GiST, SQL Server spatial indexes).
- **H3** (Uber): hexagonal hierarchical grid; uniform neighbour distances, good for aggregation and surge-pricing-style analytics.
- **S2** (Google): sphere-based cells used by many services.

Choose by query: point-nearby with simple infra (geohash in Redis/DynamoDB), polygons and complex shapes (R-tree/PostGIS), analytics and aggregation (H3).

SELECT id, name, ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint(-0.1278, 51.5074)::geography) AS metres
FROM atms
WHERE ST_DWithin(location, ST_MakePoint(-0.1278, 51.5074)::geography, 2000)
ORDER BY location <-> ST_MakePoint(-0.1278, 51.5074)::geography LIMIT 10;
~~~
~~~text
Redis: GEOADD atms -0.1278 51.5074 atm:42 ; GEOSEARCH atms FROMLONLAT -0.12 51.50 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 10
~~~
pts: Geohash prefixes give nearby cells; check neighbours at boundaries.
Quadtrees adapt to point density.
R-trees index shapes and polygons (PostGIS GiST).
H3 hexagons suit aggregation and analytics.
Choose by query type and existing infrastructure.

questions.q: You are reviewing code that uses the wrong collections. Give a decision guide for .NET collections.
questions.a:
| Need | Use | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Ordered list, index access | {{List<T>}} / arrays | LinkedList (cache misses) |
| Fast membership | {{HashSet<T>}} | {{List.Contains}} in loops |
| Key lookup | {{Dictionary<K,V>}} | Linear search over a list of pairs |
| Static lookup built once | {{FrozenDictionary}} / {{FrozenSet}} | Rebuilding dictionaries per request |
| FIFO / LIFO | {{Queue<T>}} / {{Stack<T>}} | {{RemoveAt(0)}} on lists |
| Priority scheduling, top-K | {{PriorityQueue<E,P>}} | Sorting on every insert |
| Ordered keys, ranges | {{SortedDictionary}} / {{SortedSet}} | Sorting a dictionary repeatedly |
| Concurrent key/value | {{ConcurrentDictionary}} | Dictionary + lock everywhere |
| Producer/consumer | {{Channel<T>}} | Polling loops on a ConcurrentQueue |
| Immutable snapshots | {{ImmutableArray}} / Frozen* | Exposing mutable lists |
| Large buffers | {{ArrayPool<T>}}, spans | Allocating new arrays per call |
| Read-only API surface | {{IReadOnlyList<T>}} | Returning List<T> |
pts: Lists and arrays for index access; avoid linked lists for performance.
HashSet and Dictionary for membership and lookups.
Frozen collections for static reference data.
PriorityQueue, SortedSet and Channel for scheduling, ranges and pipelines.
Expose read-only interfaces; pool large buffers.
questions.ex: A code review replacing List.Contains with a FrozenSet in a payment screening loop cut CPU for that endpoint by 70%.
fu: When is LinkedList<T> actually the right choice?
pit: Loading reference lists from the database on every request.

questions.q: Which data-structure choices matter in Angular/React front ends (normalised state, maps, virtual lists)?
questions.a:
- **Normalised state**: store entities by id ({{Record<string, Order>}} or {{Map}}) plus id arrays for order, instead of nested duplicated objects. Updates touch one place; lookups are O(1). (Redux Toolkit's {{createEntityAdapter}}, NgRx Entity.)
- **Immutable updates**: new references for changed objects so change detection (OnPush, signals, React memo) works; structural sharing keeps it cheap.
- **Sets and Maps** for selections and lookups instead of {{array.includes}} in render loops.
- **Virtualised lists** (CDK virtual scroll, react-window) render only visible rows: O(visible) DOM nodes for 100,000-row lists.
- **Memoised selectors** ({{computed}} signals, {{useMemo}}, reselect) avoid recomputing derived data.
- **Tries or indexes** for client-side typeahead over large static lists.
pts: Normalise entities by id with separate ordering arrays.
Immutable updates keep change detection correct and cheap.
Use Set and Map for selections and lookups.
Virtualise long lists to render only visible rows.
Memoise derived data with computed signals or selectors.
questions.ex: A trade blotter with 50,000 rows went from 4-second freezes to smooth scrolling after normalising state and adding virtual scrolling.
fu: When is a global store unnecessary?
pit: Deeply nested state with duplicated entities.

questions.q: Design the data structures for a limit order book with price-time priority. What are the operations and complexities?
questions.a:
Operations: add order, cancel order, match incoming orders against the best opposite price, query best bid/ask and depth.

Structures:

- **Per side, price levels in sorted order**: a sorted map (red-black tree) from price to level, or, for bounded tick ranges, an **array indexed by price tick** with a pointer to the best level (O(1) best price, very cache friendly).
- **Per price level, a FIFO queue** of orders (time priority): a linked list or array-backed queue.
- **Order id index**: hash map from order id to its node for O(1) cancel.

Complexities: add O(log P) with a tree (O(1) with tick arrays), cancel O(1), best price O(1), match O(1) per filled order.

Production concerns: single-threaded matching per instrument (deterministic, no locks), event sourcing of order events for recovery, and preallocated object pools to avoid GC pauses.

flowchart LR
  subgraph BIDS[Bids - best price first]
    B1[100.05: queue of orders in time order] --> B2[100.04: queue] --> B3[100.03: queue]
  end
  subgraph ASKS[Asks - best price first]
    A1[100.06: queue] --> A2[100.07: queue]
  end
  IDX[Dictionary order id to node, O 1 cancel] -.-> B2
  M[Incoming buy at 100.06] -->|match against best ask head first| A1
pts: Sorted price levels per side; FIFO queue per level for time priority.
Hash map from order id to node for O(1) cancels.
Tick-indexed arrays give O(1) best price for bounded ranges.
Single-threaded matching per instrument for determinism.
Event-source order events and pool objects to avoid GC pauses.
questions.ex: A crypto exchange's matching engine moved from a tree to tick-indexed arrays for liquid pairs, cutting median match latency from 9 µs to 2 µs.
fu: How do you recover the book after a crash?
pit: Using a List per level with RemoveAt for cancels (O(n)).

questions.q: How do data-structure choices drive system design? Give examples where the right structure changed the architecture.
questions.a:
Architectural decisions often reduce to "which data structure, where":

- **Rate limiting at scale**: sliding-window logs (sorted sets) vs counters vs token buckets determine memory and Redis load.
- **Leaderboards**: sorted sets (skip lists) make rank queries O(log n); a relational ORDER BY does not scale for live ranks.
- **Deduplication of events**: an exact set grows forever; a Bloom filter or time-bucketed sets bound memory with accepted error.
- **Distinct counts** for analytics: HyperLogLog turns terabytes into kilobytes, enabling real-time dashboards.
- **Sharding**: consistent hashing vs range partitioning determines rebalancing cost and hot spots.
- **Storage engines**: B-tree vs LSM-tree drives database choice for read-heavy vs write-heavy workloads.
- **Search**: inverted indexes push you to OpenSearch rather than LIKE queries.

Principal skill: recognise the structure behind the requirement and choose infrastructure that implements it natively.
questions.code:
~~~text
Requirement                                   Structure            Infrastructure that provides it
"Unique visitors per merchant, real time"      HyperLogLog          Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT
"Rank of player among 50 M, live"              Skip list/sorted set Redis ZADD/ZREVRANK
"Has this event id been processed?" (huge)     Bloom + exact store  Redis BF + DB unique key
"Distribute sessions across cache nodes"       Consistent hashing   Redis Cluster slots / client ring
"Nearby drivers"                               Geohash / R-tree     Redis GEO / PostGIS
"Full-text search with relevance"              Inverted index       OpenSearch / Azure AI Search
~~~
pts: Many architecture choices are data-structure choices in disguise.
Recognise the structure behind each requirement.
Pick infrastructure that implements it natively.
Approximate structures trade accuracy for huge memory savings.
Storage engine structure (B-tree vs LSM) drives database selection.
questions.ex: A real-time fraud dashboard became feasible only after switching distinct-card counts from SQL COUNT DISTINCT to HyperLogLog in Redis.
fu: Give an example where the wrong structure caused an outage.
pit: Treating infrastructure choices as unrelated to data structures.

questions.q: Design an in-memory rate limiter for an API gateway handling 200,000 requests per second across 10,000 API keys. Which structures?
questions.a:
Requirements: per-key limits (e.g. 1,000 requests/minute), low latency (< 50 µs per check), bounded memory, accuracy close to exact, distributed across gateway nodes.

Per node:

- **Token bucket per key**: two numbers (tokens, last refill timestamp) in a struct; O(1) check; memory ~32 bytes per key -> 10,000 keys is trivial.
- Store buckets in a **ConcurrentDictionary** or, better, **striped arrays** indexed by key hash to avoid allocation and contention; update atomically with {{Interlocked.CompareExchange}} on packed values, or lock per stripe.

Across nodes:

- **Local limits as a share** of the global limit (limit / nodes) with periodic rebalancing: no network calls per request, slight inaccuracy.
- **Central store** (Redis Lua token bucket) for exactness at the cost of a network hop; batch decrements (lease tokens in chunks of 50) to cut calls.

Evict idle keys with a timestamp wheel or periodic sweep. Return {{429}} with {{Retry-After}}.
pts: A token bucket per key is two numbers and an O(1) check.
Stripe state by key hash to reduce contention and allocation.
Local share of the global limit avoids per-request network calls.
Redis Lua buckets give exactness; lease tokens in chunks to cut round trips.
Evict idle keys and return 429 with Retry-After.
questions.ex: A gateway that called Redis on every request added 1 ms p50; leasing tokens in chunks of 50 cut Redis calls by 98% with under 2% limit overshoot.
fu: How would you implement a sliding-window log instead, and what does it cost?
pit: A global lock around all buckets.

questions.q: Your service holds a 20 GB in-memory index and suffers long GC pauses. What data-structure changes do you consider?
questions.a:
GC cost scales with the number of **live references** the GC must trace, especially in gen 2. A 20 GB heap of millions of small objects is expensive to mark.

Options:

- **Fewer, larger objects**: arrays of structs instead of object graphs; replace {{Dictionary<string, Obj>}} with struct arrays plus a compact index.
- **Avoid references inside structs** (strings) where possible: store string data in one big char/byte pool with offsets.
- **Off-heap / unmanaged memory** ({{NativeMemory.Alloc}}, memory-mapped files) for the bulk data, with a managed façade; GC no longer scans it.
- **Frozen / pinned object heap** (POH) for long-lived buffers that interop with native code.
- **GC settings**: Server GC, {{GCHeapAffinitizeMask}}, regions (default since .NET 7), concurrent GC, and DATAS for container density. Consider {{GCSettings.LatencyMode = SustainedLowLatency}} for latency-sensitive periods.
- **Move the index out of process**: Redis, a dedicated search engine, or a memory-mapped file-based index.

Measure with dotnet-counters (gc-heap-size, time-in-gc), GC traces in PerfView, and heap dumps for object counts before changing.
pts: GC cost scales with live references, not bytes alone.
Replace object graphs with struct arrays and pooled string storage.
Off-heap or memory-mapped storage removes data from GC tracing.
Tune GC mode, regions and latency modes for the workload.
Measure with counters, traces and heap dumps first.
questions.ex: A reference-data service cut gen-2 pauses from 1.8 s to 40 ms by moving 25 M instruments from objects to struct arrays with a pooled ISIN buffer.
fu: What is the Pinned Object Heap?
pit: Raising container memory limits as the only fix.

questions.q: When is it acceptable to use approximate data structures in a financial institution, and how do you govern that?
questions.a:
Acceptable where an approximate answer **informs** rather than **decides** a financial outcome, or where it filters before an exact check:

- **Analytics and dashboards**: distinct customers (HLL), top merchants (Top-K).
- **Pre-filters**: Bloom filters for "definitely not in the sanctions list hash set" **followed by an exact check** on "maybe".
- **Operational protection**: approximate rate limiting, hot-key detection.
- **Fraud features**: approximate velocity counts as model inputs, where the model tolerates noise.

Not acceptable for: balances, billing, regulatory reports, limits that are contractually binding, or any decision a customer can dispute without an exact record.

Governance:

- Document the error bounds and where each approximate structure is used (data catalogue).
- Validate periodically against exact computation (sample audits).
- Make the exact data available for disputes.
- Model-risk review when approximations feed decision models.
pts: Use approximations to inform, not to decide financial outcomes.
Pair Bloom filters with an exact check on "maybe".
Never approximate balances, billing, regulatory reports or binding limits.
Document error bounds and validate against exact computation.
Keep exact data for disputes; model-risk review where relevant.
questions.ex: A bank used Bloom-filter pre-screening to skip 97% of exact sanctions lookups while every potential match still went through the exact list and human review.
fu: How would you explain HyperLogLog error to a risk committee?
pit: Using approximate counts for fee calculations.

List.Remove inside the loop is O(m) and mutates the caller's data.

questions.q: Design a deduplication service for 1 billion events per day where each event id must be processed once within a 7-day window.
questions.a:
Scale: 1 B/day ≈ 11,600 events/s average, peaks ~50,000/s; 7 days = 7 B ids. Storing 7 B 16-byte ids exactly is ~112 GB plus overhead.

Design:

- **Exact layer**: partitioned key-value store (DynamoDB / Cassandra / Redis cluster) with conditional insert ({{attribute_not_exists}} / SET NX) and TTL 7 days. Partition by event-id hash. Conditional insert is the dedupe decision: atomic and exact.
- **Bloom-filter front layer** per time bucket (one per hour, rotating) to answer "definitely new" without hitting the store for most events; on "maybe seen", go to the exact store. At 1% false positives, about 1.2 bytes per id.
- **Time-bucketed structures**: drop whole buckets after 7 days instead of per-key expiry.
- **Stream partitioning by event id** (Kafka key) so the same id always reaches the same consumer instance: allows a local in-memory cache for very recent ids.
- **Idempotent downstream**: dedupe is defence in depth; side effects remain idempotent.
pts: Do the arithmetic: billions of ids need partitioned storage.
An exact conditional insert with TTL is the source of truth.
Time-bucketed Bloom filters skip most store calls.
Partition the stream by event id for locality.
Keep downstream side effects idempotent as defence in depth.
questions.ex: An ad-tech platform cut deduplication store costs by 80% with hourly Bloom filters in front of DynamoDB conditional writes.
fu: What happens to deduplication during a region failover?
pit: Relying on a Bloom filter alone to decide (false positives drop real events).

questions.q: How do you assess data-structure skills in candidates for Lead/Principal roles without LeetCode trivia?
questions.a:
Assess applied judgement:

- **Realistic problems**: "this reconciliation takes 11 hours; here is the code" (complexity analysis and refactoring), "design a rate limiter's state", "pick storage for a leaderboard".
- **Trade-off discussion**: ask for two approaches and when each wins (memory vs CPU, exact vs approximate, read vs write heavy).
- **Scaling the structure**: what changes at 100x data? In-memory to distributed (sharding, consistent hashing).
- **Production concerns**: concurrency, GC, persistence, failure.
- **Code review exercise**: spot wrong collections and O(n²) patterns.
- Still check fundamentals (hash tables, trees, heaps, Big-O) quickly, since they underpin every answer.

Principal signals: they quantify (back-of-envelope sizes), name the infrastructure that implements the structure, and discuss governance of approximations.

Ask for two approaches and when each wins.
Push to 100x scale and production concerns.
Include a code-review exercise.

questions.q: Hash functions in practice: when do you use non-cryptographic hashes, cryptographic hashes, HMACs and password hashes?
questions.a:
| Purpose | Use | .NET |
|---|---|---|
| Hash tables, sharding, Bloom filters, checksums for corruption | Fast non-cryptographic hash | {{XxHash64}}, {{XxHash3}}, {{Crc32}} (System.IO.Hashing) |
| Integrity against tampering, content addressing, Merkle trees | Cryptographic hash | {{SHA256.HashData}} |
| Authenticate messages with a shared secret (webhooks, API signing) | HMAC | {{HMACSHA256.HashData}} |
| Store passwords | Slow, salted password hash | PBKDF2 ({{Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2}}), ASP.NET Identity's hasher, Argon2 via libraries |
| Pseudonymise identifiers (PAN, national id) | Keyed hash (HMAC) or tokenisation | HMAC with a vault-held key |

Pitfalls: string.GetHashCode is randomised per process (never persist it); MD5/SHA-1 are broken for security; a plain SHA-256 of a card number is reversible by brute force (small space): use HMAC with a secret key or tokenisation; compare MACs with constant-time comparison ({{CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals}}).
questions.code:
~~~csharp
ulong shard = System.IO.Hashing.XxHash3.HashToUInt64(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(customerId)) % 64;    // fast, stable across processes
byte[] digest = SHA256.HashData(fileBytes);                                                          // integrity / content address
byte[] mac = HMACSHA256.HashData(webhookSecret, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(timestamp + "." + body));   // authenticity
bool valid = CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(mac, Convert.FromHexString(signatureHeader));  // constant-time compare
byte[] pwd = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations: 600_000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, outputLength: 32);
byte[] panToken = HMACSHA256.HashData(vaultKey, Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(pan));                       // keyed pseudonym, not plain SHA-256
~~~
pts: Non-cryptographic hashes for tables, sharding and filters.
SHA-256 for integrity and content addressing.
HMAC for authenticity with shared secrets; compare in constant time.
Slow salted hashes (PBKDF2, Argon2) for passwords.
Never persist string.GetHashCode; never plain-hash small spaces like PANs.
questions.ex: A team sharded data with string.GetHashCode; after a restart, keys landed on different shards. XxHash3 fixed it.
fu: Why is plain SHA-256 of a PAN unsafe?
pit: Using MD5 or unsalted SHA for passwords.

questions.q: Design the data structures for a distributed session store serving 5 million concurrent users with failover.
questions.a:
Sizing: 5 M sessions x ~2 KB = 10 GB plus overhead -> ~15 to 20 GB; with replication x2.

Structures and placement:

- **Hash of session fields** per session key ({{session:{id}}}) in Redis Cluster: O(1) access, partial updates without rewriting blobs, TTL per key (sliding expiry on activity).
- **Sharding** by hash slot (consistent placement), with replicas per shard for failover.
- **Secondary index** for "all sessions of user X" (needed for "log out everywhere"): a set per user. Put the user id in a **hash tag** in both keys ({{session:{userId}:{sid}}} and {{user-sessions:{userId}}}) so a user's sessions and index live in the same cluster slot and can be changed atomically.
- **Small, compact payloads**: ids and claims, not object graphs; MessagePack serialisation.
- **Revocation list** for JWT-based sessions if any (set with TTL = token lifetime).

Failover: replicas promote automatically; async replication can lose the last few writes (users may need to re-authenticate): acceptable for sessions, not for carts (persist carts in a database).
questions.code:
~~~text
HSET session:{u42}:s9f3 uid u42 tenant t7 roles "trader" csrf 9a1c issued 1760090000
EXPIRE session:{u42}:s9f3 1800                      # sliding: refreshed on activity
SADD user-sessions:{u42} s9f3                        # same hash tag -> same slot as the user's sessions
EXPIRE user-sessions:{u42} 86400
# log out everywhere: SMEMBERS user-sessions:{u42} -> DEL each session:{u42}:<sid> in one MULTI (same slot)
~~~
pts: Size first: 5 M sessions x 2 KB is about 10 GB before overhead and replicas.
Hash per session for partial updates and per-key TTLs.
Co-locate a user's sessions and index with hash tags.
Keep payloads compact; persist important state (carts) elsewhere.
Accept that async replication can drop the last writes on failover.
questions.ex: A trading portal implemented "log out all devices" in one atomic operation by hash-tagging session keys by user id.
fu: How would you migrate sessions between clusters without logging everyone out?
pit: Storing entire user profiles in sessions.

questions.q: Explain the inverted index and why databases struggle with full-text search. How does this shape your architecture?
questions.a:
An **inverted index** maps each term to a **postings list** of documents (and positions) containing it. Query "trail shoe" intersects the postings for "trail" and "shoe" and ranks by relevance (BM25 uses term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalisation).

Building it involves **analysis**: tokenisation, lower-casing, stemming, stop words, synonyms, n-grams for partial matching.

Relational B-tree indexes cannot serve {{LIKE '%shoe%'}} (no prefix to seek) or relevance ranking, so databases either scan or provide a separate full-text engine (SQL Server Full-Text, PostgreSQL tsvector + GIN).

Architecture: for serious search (relevance tuning, facets, typo tolerance, scale) use a dedicated engine (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Azure AI Search) fed by **CDC or outbox events**, accepting eventual consistency; keep the database as the source of truth and rebuild indexes from it.
questions.code:
~~~text
Documents:  1 "red trail shoe"   2 "blue road shoe"   3 "trail jacket"
Inverted:   red -> [1]   trail -> [1, 3]   shoe -> [1, 2]   blue -> [2]   road -> [2]   jacket -> [3]
Query "trail shoe" (AND): [1, 3] ∩ [1, 2] = [1]
~~~
~~~sql
-- PostgreSQL built-in inverted index for moderate needs
CREATE INDEX ix_products_search ON products USING gin (to_tsvector('english', name || ' ' || description));
SELECT id FROM products WHERE to_tsvector('english', name || ' ' || description) @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'trail shoe');
~~~

flowchart LR
  APP[.NET API] -->|writes| DB[(SQL database: source of truth)]
  DB -->|CDC / outbox| SYNC[Indexer]
  SYNC --> OS[(OpenSearch inverted index)]
  UI[Search UI] --> QAPI[Search API] --> OS
pts: An inverted index maps terms to postings lists of documents.
Analysis (tokenising, stemming, synonyms) shapes matching.
BM25 ranks by term frequency, rarity and length.
B-trees cannot serve contains-queries or relevance.
Use a search engine fed by CDC/outbox; the database stays the source of truth.
questions.ex: Moving product search from LIKE queries to OpenSearch cut search latency from 2.3 s to 60 ms and added typo tolerance.
fu: How do you reindex with zero downtime?
pit: Treating the search index as the system of record.

questions.q: When are lock-free data structures worth their complexity in .NET?
questions.a:
Lock-free structures use atomic operations (compare-and-swap via {{Interlocked}}) instead of locks so threads never block each other. Benefits: no deadlocks, progress under contention, lower tail latency when a lock holder could be descheduled.

Worth it when:

- Contention is high and critical sections are tiny (counters, single-producer/single-consumer queues, reference swaps).
- Latency tails matter (trading, market data, telemetry pipelines).
- You can use proven implementations: {{ConcurrentQueue}}, {{Channel}}, {{Interlocked}} counters, {{ImmutableInterlocked}} for copy-on-write swaps.

Not worth it when:

- Contention is low: a {{lock}} (especially .NET 9's {{Lock}}) is fast uncontended.
- Operations are compound and complex: correctness (ABA problem, memory ordering) is very hard to verify.

Practical approach: prefer **avoiding sharing** (partition data per thread/actor, immutable snapshots); use BCL concurrent types; write custom lock-free code only with benchmarks proving the need and stress tests (and ideally model checking).
pts: Lock-free structures use CAS instead of locks: no blocking or deadlocks.
Worth it for high contention, tiny critical sections and tail-latency goals.
Prefer BCL concurrent types and immutable snapshot swaps.
Uncontended locks are cheap; avoid custom lock-free code without evidence.
Beware ABA and memory-ordering bugs; stress test.
questions.ex: A telemetry agent replaced a locked queue with a Channel and dropped p99 enqueue latency from 2 ms to 15 µs under 64-thread contention.
fu: What is the ABA problem?
pit: Hand-rolled lock-free structures without stress tests.

questions.q: Normalised vs denormalised data: how do data-structure principles apply to database and API design?
questions.a:
Normalisation (one fact in one place) optimises **writes and consistency**; denormalisation (copies shaped for reads) optimises **reads and availability**. The same trade-off as normalised front-end state vs view models.

Guidelines:

- **System of record normalised** (relational, constraints, one owner per fact).
- **Read models denormalised** per access pattern (CQRS projections, document stores, search indexes, caches), rebuilt from the source.
- **Duplicated data needs an owner and an update path** (events, CDC) plus a staleness budget.
- **Immutable facts** (price at time of purchase) should be copied, not referenced: they must not change when the source changes.
- In NoSQL, model for access patterns (denormalise deliberately); in APIs, shape responses for consumers (BFF) rather than exposing normalised tables.
pts: Normalise the system of record for consistent writes.
Denormalise read models per access pattern.
Every copy needs an owner, an update path and a staleness budget.
Copy immutable facts like the price paid.
Shape APIs for consumers instead of exposing tables.
questions.ex: A "my orders" screen joining 7 tables at 900 ms became a single-row read at 5 ms from a projection, while the normalised order schema stayed authoritative.
fu: How do you rebuild a corrupted read model?
pit: Referencing the current product price in historical orders.

questions.q: How do you build a culture where engineers choose data structures deliberately, without micro-optimising everything?
questions.a:
- **Make complexity visible**: performance budgets per endpoint, load tests in CI on production-like data volumes, and dashboards of p95/p99 per route.
- **Review checklists** with a few data-structure questions: "lookup in a loop?", "collection sized?", "unbounded growth?", "allocation in hot path?".
- **Analysers**: Roslyn rules flagging {{List.Contains}} inside loops, missing capacity, LINQ in hot paths (where agreed).
- **Shared building blocks**: vetted caches, rate limiters, dedupe services, so teams reuse correct structures.
- **Benchmarks as artefacts**: BenchmarkDotNet results attached to performance PRs; regressions caught in CI for critical libraries.
- **Teach with incidents**: postmortems that trace back to an O(n²) or an unbounded dictionary become training material.
- **Focus on hot paths**: agree that clarity wins elsewhere.

Add a few data-structure questions to review checklists.
Provide vetted shared building blocks.
Benchmark critical paths and gate regressions in CI.
Optimise hot paths; keep clarity elsewhere.

questions.q: Summarise how a Principal Engineer thinks about data structures.

"I treat data structures as the core of system design, not an interview topic:

- I start from the access pattern and the numbers: size, read/write ratio, latency target, concurrency.

Map structures to infrastructure that implements them.
Approximate structures inform, never decide money.
Normalised sources, denormalised read models, shared defaults.

questions.q: How do you compute p99 latency or the median transaction amount over billions of values and across many servers? Explain quantile sketches (t-digest, DDSketch, HDR histograms) and why you cannot average percentiles.
questions.a:
### The problem
Exact percentiles need all values sorted, which is impossible for unbounded streams and expensive across a fleet. And **averaging p99s from 50 servers is mathematically wrong**: the fleet p99 is not the mean of per-server p99s.

### Sketches: small, mergeable summaries
| Structure | Idea | Guarantee | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HDR histogram** | fixed buckets with configurable significant digits | relative error bounded by precision setting | very fast, fixed memory for a value range; widely used for latency |
| **t-digest** | clusters of points, finer resolution at the tails | very accurate at extreme quantiles in practice | mergeable; good for amounts and latencies |
| **DDSketch** | logarithmic buckets | **relative-error guarantee** (for example 1%) for every quantile | fully mergeable, used by observability vendors |
| **KLL / GK sketches** | rank-error guarantees | bounded rank error | streaming databases |
| Prometheus native or exponential histograms | exponential buckets | relative error by scale | server-side quantile computation |

**Mergeability** is the key property: each server keeps its own sketch, and sketches are merged (not averaged) to get fleet-wide quantiles.

### Uses in banking systems
Latency SLOs (p99 per endpoint), fraud features (a customer's 95th-percentile spend as a baseline), anomaly detection on transaction amounts, and reporting medians over billions of rows in analytics engines (approximate percentile functions use these sketches).
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  S1[Server 1 sketch] --> M[Merge sketches]
  S2[Server 2 sketch] --> M
  S3[Server 50 sketch] --> M
  M --> Q[Fleet p50, p99, p99.9 with bounded error]
  X[Average of per-server p99s] -.->|wrong| Q
pts: Exact percentiles do not scale; sketches summarise in small memory.
HDR histograms, t-digest, DDSketch, KLL.
Mergeable: combine sketches, never average percentiles.
DDSketch gives relative-error guarantees.

questions.q: How do vector indexes work (HNSW graphs, IVF, product quantisation, DiskANN), and how do their parameters trade recall, latency and memory?
questions.a:
### Why approximate
Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector: O(n x d). With 50 million 1,536-dimension vectors that is far too slow, so systems use **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes and measure **recall** (share of true neighbours found).

### The main index families
| Index | How it works | Strengths | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world) | multi-layer proximity graph; search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily descends | excellent recall and latency, incremental inserts | memory heavy (vectors plus graph links), slow builds, deletes are awkward |
| **IVF** (inverted file) | k-means clusters; search only the nprobe nearest clusters | smaller memory, fast builds | recall depends on nprobe; needs training |
| **PQ / scalar or binary quantisation** | compress vectors into codes | 4 to 32x less memory | lower accuracy; often rescored with full vectors |
| **DiskANN / Vamana** | graph index designed for SSDs | billions of vectors with small RAM | SSD latency, complex tuning |

### HNSW parameters
- {{M}}: links per node. Higher means better recall and more memory.
- {{ef_construction}}: candidate list during build. Higher means better graph quality and slower builds.
- {{ef_search}}: candidate list at query time. Higher means better recall and more latency; tune per query class.

### Practical tuning
Measure recall@k against exact search on a sample of real queries, then pick the cheapest settings that meet the target (for example recall@10 of at least 0.95 at p95 under 50 ms). Combine with filters carefully: restrictive filters can starve the graph search, so use databases that apply filters inside the index traversal (pre-filtering) or increase ef for filtered queries.

questions.q: Which CRDT data types exist (counters, registers, sets, sequences), how does each merge, and where would you use them in banking-adjacent systems?
questions.a:
### What makes a CRDT
Conflict-free replicated data types let replicas update independently and **always converge** when they exchange state or operations, because merges are commutative, associative and idempotent. No coordination at write time.

### Common types
| Type | State | Merge | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G-Counter** | one count per replica | per-replica maximum, value = sum | page views, approximate usage counters |
| **PN-Counter** | two G-Counters (increments, decrements) | merge each, value = P - N | likes, inventory adjustments where negatives are acceptable |
| **LWW-Register** | value plus timestamp | keep the latest timestamp | user profile fields where last edit wins |
| **MV-Register** | all concurrent values | keep concurrent siblings | surface conflicts to the user |
| **G-Set / 2P-Set** | added (and removed) sets | union | tags; 2P-Set cannot re-add removed items |
| **OR-Set** (observed-remove) | elements with unique tags | add wins over concurrent remove | shopping baskets, device lists, preferences |
| **RGA / sequence CRDTs** | ordered elements with ids | interleave by ids | collaborative text editing |

### Where they fit and where they do not
- Fit: offline-first apps (adviser tablets syncing), multi-region caches and session state, collaboration features, counters for rate limiting or metrics in active-active setups.
- Do **not** fit invariants: "balance must never go below zero" cannot be maintained by a counter that merges independently; two regions can each approve a withdrawal. Money movements need coordination (a single writer per account, consensus, or escrow-style reservations that split the allowed amount between regions).

### Complexity table
| Structure | Lookup | Insert | Delete | Ordered | .NET |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Array/List | O(1) index, O(n) search | O(1)* end, O(n) middle | O(n) | by index | List<T>, T[] |
| Hash table | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | no | Dictionary, HashSet, Frozen* |
| Red-black tree | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | yes | SortedDictionary, SortedSet |
| Sorted array | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) | yes | SortedList |
| Binary heap | min O(1) | O(log n) | O(log n) | partial | PriorityQueue |
| Linked list | O(n) | O(1) at node | O(1) at node | insertion | LinkedList (rarely best) |

### Patterns
Complement lookup (two-sum) · sliding window · two pointers · prefix sums (+ Fenwick/segment tree when updating) · BFS (shortest hops) / DFS (components, cycles) · topological sort (Kahn) · Dijkstra (non-negative), Bellman-Ford (negative, arbitrage) · Union-Find (incremental connectivity) · size-K heap for top-K · interval merge with half-open ranges.

### System structures
B+tree (OLTP indexes) vs LSM-tree (write-heavy) · Bloom filter (~9.6 bits/item @1%) · HyperLogLog (0.81% in 12 KB) · Count-Min (never under) · consistent hashing + vnodes · skip list (Redis ZSET) · ring buffer · Merkle tree · inverted index · geohash/R-tree/H3 · W-TinyLFU.

### .NET performance
Pre-size collections · CollectionsMarshal spans/refs · structs and struct arrays · FrozenDictionary for static data · ConcurrentDictionary + Lazy for single creation · Channels for pipelines · avoid GC-heavy object graphs for huge in-memory indexes.

### Say this
"Access pattern first, then structure, then infrastructure." "Big-O hides constants and cache misses." "Approximate structures inform, never decide money." "Normalised source, denormalised read models."

### Added essentials
- **Hash tables**: load factor drives chain length; resize is O(n) but amortised O(1); pre-size; HashCode.Combine over equality fields; string hashes are randomised per process.
- **Bitmaps**: exact set membership at 1 bit per id; roaring bitmaps compress sparse sets; fast AND/OR for segments and posting lists.
- **Pictures to remember**: LRU = dictionary plus doubly linked list; B+tree leaves linked for range scans; Bloom filter = k bits, "no" is certain; W-TinyLFU = window plus admission filter plus segmented LRU; order book = sorted price levels with FIFO queues plus id index.
